# SK4033 — The `ConcurrentDictionary` member taken is the expensive one

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`dict.Keys.Count` locks the whole table and copies every key into a new list to produce a number `dict.Count` already has; `dict.Count == 0` locks it to answer what `dict.IsEmpty` answers for free.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Performance |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | SK1034 |

## Why

On every other dictionary `Keys` and `Values` are views and `Count` is a field read. On this one they are neither. `ConcurrentDictionary.Keys` acquires every lock in the table and copies the whole collection into a fresh `List<TKey>` before the caller reads anything at all, so `dict.Keys.Count` is a locking O(n) allocation. `Count` acquires every lock as well, because a consistent total means stopping the table. `IsEmpty` acquires nothing and allocates nothing. The receiver is what makes the difference enormous rather than marginal, and it is invisible in the shape of the call — which is exactly why it is worth a rule.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (cache.Keys.Count > 0) {
    Flush(cache);
}

if (pending.Count == 0) {
    return;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
if (!cache.IsEmpty) {
    Flush(cache);
}

if (pending.IsEmpty) {
    return;
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`SK1034` reads `dict.Keys.Count()` and offers `dict.Keys.Count`, which is right and leaves the expensive half standing.** This rule reports on the same span and declares `supersedes: ["SK1034"]`, so where both fire the stronger remedy wins and the weaker one stays in the report marked superseded rather than disappearing. Matching the span is the whole mechanism — `Supersession.Apply` pairs findings by rule, file, line and column — which is why `SK1034` runs inside this batch's own test list. The one shape where the two spans do not coincide is a mirrored comparison, `0 < dict.Keys.Count()`, where both are reported; both are true and neither is wrong. ⚠ **`dict.Keys.Contains(k)` looks like it belongs here and does not, and this is the useful exclusion.** `Keys` hands back a plain `List<TKey>`, whose `Contains` uses `EqualityComparer<TKey>.Default`, while `ContainsKey` uses the comparer the dictionary was *constructed* with. For a table built with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` the two give different answers, and nothing at the call site says which kind of table this is — so the obvious rewrite is a behaviour change wearing a performance fix's clothes. ⚠ Only comparisons with `0`, or with `1` under `<`/`>=`, are read as emptiness tests; a count is never negative, so those are the only ones a comparison with a literal decides. Anything else is a claim about *how many*, which `IsEmpty` cannot answer. ⚠ `Any()` becomes `!dict.IsEmpty`, which is a unary expression where the call was a primary one, so it is offered only where the surrounding syntax cannot re-bind — the same restriction and the same list as `SK1034`. `dict.Keys.Any().ToString()` would otherwise become `!dict.IsEmpty.ToString()`, which parses, binds, and means something else. The `!dict.Keys.Any()` form has no such restriction, because `dict.IsEmpty` is primary too. ⚠ The receiver must be a path of names, since the fix writes it a second time. ⚠ `LongCount()` is left alone: it returns `long` where `Count` returns `int`, and a narrowing of the static type can change which overload a surrounding call resolves to.
